name: composite
intent: Compose objects into tree structures that represent part-whole hierarchies: leaves implement the shared Component operations directly, containers implement them by delegating to their children and combining the results, so a client invokes one operation once and it applies uniformly to a single object or an arbitrarily deep composition.
problem: Code that handles a hierarchy of containers and primitives has to know which is which: every traversal, aggregation, rendering or serialisation routine needs type tests for the container case, and the same distinction is re-implemented wherever the structure is used. Adding a new node kind then means editing every one of those routines.
context: Applies wherever the domain is genuinely a tree of things-that-contain-things - file systems, UI widget trees, document/XML/YAML trees, expression and query trees, build task graphs, bundles of priced items - and the client wants to invoke one operation over any part of it. The pattern also assumes the tree is the unit of composition (not a shared graph) and that the operation is meaningful for both a leaf and a container.
benefits: Clients treat leaves and containers uniformly: one call site handles a primitive node and an arbitrarily deep subtree, so tag-and-switch logic disappears from client code.
Recursive behaviour is expressed once, in the container's implementation, instead of being re-written by every consumer of the structure.
New node kinds are added by implementing the component interface; existing clients and traversals stay untouched (open/closed).
Substructures can be built, moved or reused as values: a composite can be passed, stored and composed wherever a single component is expected.
Operations that must apply to the whole tree (validate, render, serialise, size, discount) are naturally defined as whole-tree operations rather than repeated per-node loops.
Tests can substitute a one-child container for a leaf (and vice versa), which makes the uniform contract cheap to pin down.
tradeoffs: The uniform interface has to be the lowest common denominator: operations that make sense only for containers (add/remove/getChild) either move up into Component and make leaves lie, or stay on the container and force clients to distinguish after all - the transparency-vs-safety trade-off is unavoidable, not a detail.

Dynamic dispatch plus per-node indirection costs more than a flat collection: each node is usually a separate allocation reached through a pointer or a vtable, so cache behaviour degrades on large trees.

Ownership becomes a design problem: a node must not be owned by two parents, shared subtrees turn a tree into a DAG (reference counting, cycles, weak back-pointers), and deep trees make recursive destruction and traversal a stack-depth hazard.
Debugging and profiling follow indirection: a stack trace crosses N recursive calls with no visual indication of the tree position, and deep structures are awkward in debuggers.
The pattern is easy to over-apply: a one-level structure or a hierarchy with a single container kind is heavier than a plain collection plus a function.

participants.responsibility: Declares the interface common to leaves and containers (the operations clients invoke uniformly) and, in the transparent design, the child-management operations as well; clients are written against this type only.
Represents a primitive node with no children and implements the component operations directly - usually the place where the real work happens.

Represents an inner node: stores its child Components, implements the component operations by delegating to those children and combining their results, and (in the safe design) owns the child-management operations.
Builds and works with the tree exclusively through Component; it must not depend on concrete node classes except at the few sites that change the structure.

use_cases: File-system-like trees: a Directory and a File answer the same size()/walk() call, so reports and copies run over any subtree without knowing node kinds.
UI widget trees: a panel and a single control share show/hide/move/render, which makes group operations over a selection trivial.

Expression and query trees: an operand and an operator node both evaluate, so arithmetic ASTs, filter trees and expression-tree compilers (for example LINQ's System.Linq.Expressions) can be translated recursively.
Document and markup models: sections contain paragraphs contain spans, and validation, search or serialisation apply to the whole part-whole hierarchy uniformly.
Build and task graphs: a task is either an atomic step or a sequence/group of tasks, so scheduling and reporting are written once.
Priced bundles: an order line and a bundle of order lines compute their price, tax and discount through the same call, which keeps promotion logic in one place.

React / Vue / Angular component trees: a container component and a leaf component share a render() contract, enabling recursive composition of forms, menus, and panel hierarchies without type branching in rendering logic.

Document Object Model (DOM) in JavaScript: every DOM node shares an appendChild()/removeChild()/querySelectorAll() interface, and the browser engine recursively renders the entire tree through one uniform call path.
Python AST (Abstract Syntax Tree) parsing: ast.NodeVisitor walks a tree of module/function/expr/constant nodes uniformly; a new analysis pass is a new visitor, not a modification of the node classes.

XML/YAML document models: element trees parsed from untrusted input must implement uniform traversal but also apply security controls (entity expansion limits, depth limits) — the Composite interface coexists with these safeguards.
Organizational hierarchies: Manager and IndividualContributor share an Employee interface with a getSalary() and getSubordinates() operation, enabling total payroll aggregation over the whole tree.
Menu and navigation trees: MenuGroup and MenuItem both satisfy a renderable() contract, so the router renders the full navigation tree without querying node types.

three.js scene graph: every node is an Object3D (Mesh, Group, Light, Camera) sharing add()/remove()/traverse(), and world transforms are computed by recursively composing each node's local matrix with its parent's via updateMatrixWorld() - a Group and a single Mesh are rendered through the same recursive path.

Unity Transform hierarchy: every GameObject owns a Transform that can have a parent and children; SetParent()/DetachChildren() restructure the tree and position/rotation/scale cascade from parent to descendants, so one operation on a root moves the whole subtree.

Java Swing containment hierarchy: JComponent extends Container, so buttons and panels alike are Components in a single tree; painting, layout and event dispatch recurse through the containment hierarchy regardless of whether a node is a leaf control or a nested panel.
avoid_when: The structure is a single flat level: a collection plus a function over it is smaller and clearer than an abstraction layer.
There is exactly one leaf kind and one container kind and no prospect of another: two functions over a sealed type (or a struct with a slice) do the same job with less machinery.

The operations are not in fact common to leaves and containers - if clients must branch per node kind anyway, a plain tagged union with a switch, or several focused operations, is more honest than a forced interface.

The relationships form a graph or DAG with shared nodes and back-pointers: model that explicitly (shared ownership plus weak back-references, or an index-based graph) instead of pretending it is a tree.
Traversal is the hot path and per-node pointer chasing dominates: a flattened, contiguous representation (arrays of nodes plus index children) is faster and still supports the same operations.
The 'uniform' operation would have to hide real differences in node semantics (different validation rules, incompatible units); separate operations with explicit types beat one interface with flags.
anti_patterns: "God component": Every operation any node kind might need is pushed onto Component, so leaves accumulate empty, throwing or silently-ignoring methods and the interface stops describing a contract.
Type tags instead of polymorphism: Nodes carry a kind field and clients chain if (node.kind == ...) tests before every operation, which is the duplication the pattern exists to remove.
Exposing the live child collection: Any caller can mutate the tree behind the container's back, invalidating invariants (ordering, uniqueness, parent links).
Applying Composite to flat data: Wrapping a list of records in Leaf/Composite classes when a plain collection and a loop were enough.
Shared subtrees without an ownership model: Two parents reference the same child; mutation on one side surprises the other and destruction double-frees or leaks.

XML bomb / billion-laughs vulnerability: Deserialising a Composite tree from untrusted XML/YAML without disabling entity expansion or setting depth limits; a few-hundred-byte payload can exhaust gigabytes of memory. Mitigate with defusedxml, JAXP FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING, or parser-level entity-expansion caps.

Prop-explosion API: In React/UI frameworks, adding boolean and string props for every structural variation instead of using compound components; callers cannot control layout without requesting new props, and the component accumulates impossible state combinations.
design_principles: Program to an interface, not an implementation: clients depend on Component, never on leaf or container classes.
Open/closed principle: new node kinds are added by implementing Component, without editing clients or traversals.
Single responsibility: leaves compute, containers compose - a node that does both usually wants to be two nodes.
Liskov substitution: a container must be usable wherever a leaf is expected; this is exactly what child management on Component threatens.
Composition over inheritance: the tree is formed by containment and delegation, not by deepening the class hierarchy.
Encapsulate what varies: node kinds and traversal strategies vary behind one stable interface while clients stay fixed.
best_practices: Put on Component only the operations that are meaningful for every node; keep add/remove/getChild on the container and provide isComposite()/asComposite() for the rare structural edits.
Enforce single ownership so that the structure stays a tree; if sharing is required, model it explicitly with shared references and weak links back to the parent.
Reject self-insertion and ancestor insertion when adding children — cycles turn every traversal into non-termination.
Expose children as a read-only view or a copy, and validate on insertion (no null children, no duplicates if the domain forbids them).
Provide one traversal (iterator, visitor or walk method) instead of letting every client re-implement recursion, and prefer an explicit stack when depth depends on untrusted input.
Test leaves and containers against the same contract - a one-child container must behave like its child, and an empty container must still satisfy the operation's identity case.
Keep the identity case of each operation explicit (empty sum = 0, empty render = empty document) so containers degrade gracefully.
Prefer immutable trees when the structure is shared across threads; rebuild subtrees on edit rather than mutating in place — avoids synchronization bugs entirely.
Use @cached_property (Python) or equivalent memoization for expensive aggregate operations (total_size, word_count) on immutable trees; add explicit invalidation when the tree is mutable.
For deep trees (hundreds of levels), replace recursive traversal with an explicit stack to avoid hitting Python's recursion limit (~1000 frames by default).
Protect aggregate operations against O(n²) recomputation: cache roll-ups or compute once per traversal, and measure before adding complexity.
Prefer Protocol (Python) over ABC when duck-typing is sufficient; use ABC only when isinstance checks or shared default behaviour are genuinely needed.

In languages with algebraic data types or discriminated unions (TypeScript, Python + match, Rust enum), prefer a closed sum-type tree representation over a class hierarchy when node kinds are fixed — the type checker flags missing pattern matches via assert_never() equivalents.

When building trees from untrusted input (e.g. parsed XML, JSON, YAML), validate invariants (no cycles, no duplicate children, depth limits) at construction time; do not rely on lazy validation during traversal.
Keep the component interface small (3–7 operations); if it grows beyond that, split into separate interfaces or move operations into separate traversal services rather than bloating the Component.

Use a Builder or Configurer (separate from Client) to construct complex trees — separates construction semantics from computation semantics and prevents partially-formed trees from escaping construction.

In React or similar UI frameworks, compound components (parent providing state via context, children consuming it) are the idiomatic Composite variant — avoid prop-explosion by letting callers compose structure rather than configure it.

For XML/JSON/YAML serialization of tree structures from untrusted sources, disable DTD processing, forbid entity expansion, and set parse-depth and output-size limits to prevent billion-laughs and quadratic-blowup attacks.

pitfalls: Declaring child management on Component so that leaves must implement meaningless add/remove methods — the interface stops meaning anything and LSP breaks.
Letting one node be a child of two parents without an ownership rule: the same subtree is destroyed twice or mutated from one side of the tree.
Allowing a node to be inserted into its own descendant, which turns traversal into infinite recursion.
Exposing the live child collection so any caller can mutate the tree behind the container's back, invalidating invariants (ordering, uniqueness, parent links).
Applying Composite to flat data: wrapping a list of records in Leaf/Composite classes when a plain collection and a loop were enough.
Shared subtrees without an ownership model: two parents referencing the same child, so mutation on one side surprises the other and destruction double-frees or leaks.

Deep recursion hitting language limits: Python's default recursion limit (~1000 frames) causes RecursionError on trees deeper than that; use iterative traversal with an explicit stack for untrusted depth.

O(n²) aggregation without caching: repeated tree walks that recompute the same aggregate (e.g., total price called per parent) degrade sharply on large trees; cache on immutable trees or compute once per traversal.

Accidentally sharing a mutable children list across multiple container instances: if two composites use the same list reference, mutations bleed between them — always initialise children with a fresh list per instance.

XML/XXE/billion-laughs attacks when deserialising tree structures from untrusted XML or YAML: malicious deeply nested entity definitions or YAML anchors can exhaust CPU and memory within seconds. Mitigations: disable DTDs, forbid entity expansion, set parse-depth and output-size limits (see defusedxml, JAXP FSP, OWASP XML cheat sheet).

Forcing a DAG or graph into a tree mental model: when nodes can have multiple parents or cycles are legitimate, Composite is the wrong abstraction — use an explicit graph model with reference counting or visited sets in every traversal.

Bloating the Component interface with domain operations that only some node kinds need, producing 'God component' — leaves accumulate empty/throwing stubs and clients lose the uniform contract guarantee.

Mutable shared state across threads without synchronisation: a mutable composite tree is not thread-safe; either make the tree immutable (rebuild on edit) or isolate mutations behind a single-threaded owner (actor-style).

Using transparent Composite (child management on Component) when safety is more important than uniformity — every Leaf must define meaningful behaviour for add/remove, which violates LSP and produces misleading APIs.

Constructing a tree from untrusted input without validating invariants: null children, duplicate children, self-insertion, and cycles should be rejected at construction time, not during the first traversal.

Wrong move: enforcing child-type rules ('no folders inside folders', 'a Section may only contain Blocks') with instanceof tests inside the container's add() -> adding a new node kind forces an edit to every container and every rule chain, breaking open/closed -> instead express placement rules as a validator or policy supplied at construction, or split the model into distinct node interfaces so the type system rejects illegal children statically.

Wrong move: trusting the uniform interface to cover operations leaves genuinely cannot honour -> clients that hold a Component reference call the method in good faith and hit a runtime throw or silent no-op on exactly the nodes that look interchangeable -> instead keep Component to operations every node can implement meaningfully and reach container-only behaviour through an explicit asComposite()/isComposite() view, so the split is checked at compile time or at one visible site.

Wrong move: mutating the child collection while a recursive traversal is iterating it (adding/removing nodes from inside a traverse callback) -> the walk skips nodes, visits freed ones, or throws a concurrent-modification error (three.js explicitly discourages graph edits during traverse) -> instead snapshot the child list before iterating, or queue structural edits and apply them once the traversal completes.

related_patterns_notes.decorator: Both Composite and Decorator rely on recursive composition. Composite builds trees of objects; Decorator wraps a single object to add behaviour. The intents differ but the structures are structurally similar, and the two patterns are often used together (decorating a subtree without changing its type).
related_patterns_notes.visitor: Visitor adds operations to a stable Composite tree without changing the node classes themselves — a new operation is a new Visitor subclass, not a new node. Composite can be traversed with Visitor when many operations must be applied to the same fixed tree structure.
related_patterns_notes.iterator: Iterator provides a way to traverse a Composite without exposing its internal storage. Use when clients need to walk the tree without knowing whether children are stored as list, tree, or other structure.
related_patterns_notes.flyweight: Both patterns share the idea of recursive composition. Flyweight conserves memory by sharing repeated leaf data across many nodes; Composite can use Flyweight to represent shared subtrees or repeated leaf content without deep copying.
related_patterns_notes.chain-of-responsibility: Often used with Composite: a leaf component that cannot handle a request passes it to its parent, traversing up the parent chain to the root. The Composite provides the natural parent-link backbone for the chain.
related_patterns_notes.whole-part: Synonymous with Composite in many OOP contexts — the whole-part hierarchy is the defining structure of the pattern.
related_patterns_notes.null-object: An empty Composite (no children) can act as a Null Object for the Component interface: it satisfies the contract with identity behaviour (e.g., sum = 0, render = empty), avoiding null checks in client code.
related_patterns_notes.builder: Builder is frequently paired with Composite to construct complex trees step-by-step, especially when validation must occur during construction rather than after. The Builder is the 'Configurer' that is the brain of a well-formed tree.
related_patterns_notes.interpreter: Interpreter is Composite applied to language representation: an AST is a tree of expression nodes where each node evaluates itself recursively. In Python, the two patterns collapse into frozen dataclasses plus recursive match functions.
related_patterns_notes.compound-components: The React/Vue compound-components pattern (implicit shared state via context, children assembled by the caller) is a language-specific realisation of the Composite pattern where the Component interface is split across a Provider and multiple child consumers connected by context.
